newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysian stocks fall seen unearthing bargains.
newsitem.headline: Malaysian stocks fall seen unearthing bargains.

text.p: A 3.3 percent slump on the key Kuala Lumpur stock index on Monday, precipitated by Wall Street's fall on Friday, has made several Malaysian blue-chip stocks into bargains, analysts said.

At the close of trade on Monday, the benchmark Composite Index of 100 large-capitalised stocks fell 37.27 points, or 3.27 percent, to 1,101.09, its lowest in seven-and-a-half months. It hit a low of 1,097.98 earlier on Monday.

Fund managers said the decline is not prompting them to sell, and instead are urging clients to pick up attractively valued stocks in industries like consumer products, construction and financial services.
"We're not panicking here," said Robert Coombe, executive director at Commerce Asset Fund Managers in Kuala Lumpur.
"If you're not geared and not in the Second Board (of small-cap stocks), you should be buying," he added.
Wall Street's Dow Jones index fell 2.3 percent on Friday .

"The Dow definitely made the sentiment worse," said Ang Kok Heng, general manager at TA Asset Management. "I think the market is coming to a bottom, but it's hard to say if a sharp technical rebound will come in. If the Dow stabilises, but doesn't rebound, I think the market will be sideways," he said.

Bulls in the Kuala Lumpur market had already been scarce since the central bank's restrictions on property and stock lending at the end of March raised questions about profits in both sectors. From March 28 through Friday, Malaysian blue-chip stocks fell 6.5 percent.

Malaysia's move to curb speculation in the property market followed similar actions in neighbouring Thailand and Singapore. The Philippine stock market has also been convulsed by fear of a property glut.
"A few panic sellers can really scare the market," said Simon Maughan, head of research at W.I. Carr. "The biggest problem is convincing people that they should buy now."

He said stocks he still recommends are in the "emerging blue-chip" group, such as car distributor Edaran Otomobil Nasional Bhd (EON). Valuing EON just on its motor business, the stock is selling at a 40 percent discount to its peers, said Maughan.
Other stocks he recommends are insurer Malaysian Assurance Alliance Bhd, construction firm Road Builder (M) Holdings Bhd, and Malaysia Mining Corp Bhd.
"The Kuala Lumpur market had a good year last year (so) that people have forgotten things can get bad again," said Coombe.
"Our advice to investors is to hold in there. We're not anticipating a crash, but it's going to be a saw-tooth pattern emerging in the next two to three months," he said.

"With a prospective 1997 p.e. (price-earnings multiple) of around 18 times, you can't go wrong," said Ramlan Ahmad, senior manager at Commerce MGI fund managers. Analysts said the market has historically traded at levels of 20 to 21 times.
Coombe said some sectors his firm is investing in are so-called defensive industries -- those whose earnings are resilient through economic cycles -- like consumer goods makers and utilities.
But investors should be picky, he said. Compared with other regional markets, "Malaysia is not cheap", said Coombe.
Ang said there are "lots of bargains" for investors who do not have to sell to cover leveraged positions.
"Some blue chips like Telekom have dropped," said Ang, adding that food second-liners include hotel and property firm Pernas International Holdings Bhd.
Other stocks on his buy list include Affin Holdings Bhd and construction company Sungei Way Holdings Bhd.
-- Kuala Lumpur newsroom (603-206 2323)
